title: Argos Evolve
author: argos-evolve
selftext:
\# Argos Evolve — an open-source, LLM-native 2D game engine (fork it for your own games)



Hi all. I've been thinking of building a 2D top down game for a while and could picture the process. Pick a game engine, learn it, strap on Claude, push for changes, see errors, fix errors, rinse and repeat. Then it clicked: instead of using AI from the outside of the engine, I should make an engine where the AI was inside the engine.



I wanted to move fast, and have the LLM do all the coding with rapid self-correction and minimal token use. I realised that perhaps a better way would be to design Claude or an LLM to be like a conductor, and for me to simply watch and provide feedback. So I started developing Argos, the hundred-eyed giant from Greek mythology.



The idea was Argos could see every part of the code quickly. Errors were short and meaningful and piped straight to the LLM. Objects, enemies, everything, had a fingerprint which told the LLM where the item was, its stats, how to update etc. Super rapid iteration. No searching through documentation and wasting tokens and time to make changes. (See screenshot of me fixing an issue in the game.)



I realised as I did this that a huge amount of todo items were quickly being created so I added the "Evolve" part, which presents the user with items that are not currently working. These are presented as a direct LLM prompt to the user. Copy to clipboard, paste to Claude. The last part of the prompt is "Remove this item from the evolve list once done". Speed is key.



So we have \*\*Argos Evolve\*\*.



Another idea I had was because AI was already in the engine, why not use it as an antagonist? I created something called the "Overseer" which sees when I'm bored and generates events, such as a boss spawn. A green LED light flashes when the Overseer is thinking up something evil. It currently uses gemma e2b to spawn stuff but you can use an API once again.



\---



Once the basics were working I realised there were other cool things that made a lot of sense to lock in:



The camera differences between 2D genres are reasonably small. You can lock in the camera for space invaders, enable the X axis for Mario, or unlock zoom and the x,y axis for an open world system.



What about Tetris? That's blocks falling into place. But so is an inventory system, and the backpack in the open world game needs that too. Done.



\- Minimap? Check.

\- Resource nodes / harvesting? Check.

\- Wall collisions, floor tiles, fog of war? Check, check, check.

\- Score, lives, XP/levels, shields, power-ups, roguelike loop? All check.

\- Multiplayer? Already in there - one machine hosts, others join over LAN. Early days, but it's intentionally integrated to save headaches later.



Then I got sick of copying and pasting the evolve prompt system so I made the world terminal. Hit Shift + \~ and the game pauses. You can prompt each item, enemy, resource, etc. Ask to change it, update it, all inside the game. The world terminal connects via an API to an LLM (I'm using deepseek 4 flash) and acts like a CLI.



I then started adding "select all" features, cut and paste features etc, and realised I was digging myself quite a rabbit hole. Which takes me to releasing this...



I can't keep working on it right now but figured that instead of it sitting in a private repo for a year, I may as well just pass it on. Maybe someone thinks this is a cool idea and wants to fork it?



Caveats? It's raw. I've done my best to make the foundation strong and limit divergence from what the engine should do. I'm at a crossroads with it though: push primitives and it becomes a solid arcade game generator, or diverge from primitives and build something larger of my own. Whoever picks it up gets to decide which way it goes.



If you do decide to have a go, I recommend clicking Build>Horde Survival as this uses the whole loop: (prompt → composed game → live play → LLM inspect/fix). Start there to see how it all fits together.



Oh, and I picked all the components of the engine so it ports to pretty much everything. Happy to answer any questions.



\---



Other geeky stuff below which I got Claude to write up for you:



The core principle is a hard separation between \*\*a compiled, deterministic C++ runtime\*\* and \*\*an LLM orchestration layer\*\*. The LLM never writes raw frame-loop C++. Instead it composes games from a frozen vocabulary of engine \*\*primitives\*\* — movement models, behaviors, tile roles, win/loss conditions, spawn rules — expressed as validated JSON + bounded Lua. If the LLM proposes something invalid, the engine rejects it rather than crashing. The simulation runs locally at \*\*zero token cost\*\*; the LLM is only invoked at meaningful moments (a death, a wave clear, your feedback).



This keeps generated games cheap, safe, and replayable, and means a game is a \~143 KB text blueprint you can share without shipping native code.



\## What it can do



Those camera/axis choices are part of a small taxonomy — camera, play mode, spatial model, scroll direction, movement preset — and combinations of those five fields cover a lot of 2D ground:



\- Top-down survivors / shooters (Vampire Survivors-style)

\- Side-scrollers (Mario-style platformers)

\- Fixed-screen arcade (Space Invaders, Frogger, Pac-Man-style)

\- Grid/puzzle systems (inventory-as-puzzle, Tetris-style falling blocks)

\- Maze, arena, defend-the-point, and more



In every case the Build menu takes a natural-language description, has the LLM compose it, and runs a deterministic playtest gate that verifies the game actually works before it ships.



\## Batteries included — the LLM doesn't rebuild the wheel every time



Worth spelling out the token angle on those primitives above. They're pre-coded, compiled C++, deterministic, and already tested, so the LLM just \*plugs them in\* — it never re-implements (or re-debugs) a minimap, an inventory, or collision handling from one build to the next. Contrast that with the "AI writes raw code" tools, which regenerate all of that from scratch every time, burning tokens and reintroducing the same class of bugs. In Argos the model spends its tokens on \*what makes your game yours\* — the composition, the tuning, the feel. When a primitive you need doesn't exist yet, that's the one case it gets built, and then it joins the library too (the evolve queue).



\## Which models?



Bring your own. Generation runs through a provider abstraction, so you can use a cloud API (\*\*DeepSeek\*\*, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter) or a \*\*fully local model via \[Ollama\](https://ollama.com)\*\* — same compose pipeline either way. DeepSeek is the cheapest reliable cloud option I've tested. Local generation works too, but be honest with yourself about model size: a strong local model composes fine, while very small models (e.g. a 2B) often can't follow the structured output the validation gate requires, and the build will fail cleanly rather than ship something broken. Either way, \*\*the simulation itself runs with zero model calls\*\* — the LLM is only touched at build time and at discrete moments while you play.



\## "Why not just use HTML/JS game frameworks?"



Fair question — and if you want a quick browser game, use them. Argos exists for a different reason:



\- \*\*The LLM doesn't write the game loop.\*\* Browser-based "AI makes a game" tools have the model emit raw JS every time, which is fragile — one bad token and the whole thing breaks. Argos restricts the LLM to a \*validated vocabulary of primitives\*. Invalid output is rejected, not run. The compiled C++ runtime is the same every time; only safe, bounded data changes.

\- \*\*It's deterministic and replayable.\*\* A fixed-tick native simulation means the same inputs always produce the same result — required for replay, debugging, and \*\*server-authoritative multiplayer\*\*. Most web/canvas AI-game demos are single-player and non-deterministic by nature.

\- \*\*Zero-cost local play.\*\* The game, once built, runs natively with no model calls. You're not burning tokens (or waiting on a server) every frame.

\- \*\*Native performance & a path to ship.\*\* C++/SDL3, headed for desktop/console rather than a tab — hundreds of entities without GC stutter.

\- \*\*You and the model grow one engine together.\*\* Pause, click any unit/tile, ask the model what's going on, change it live, save. Capability gaps you hit are logged and become things you can build. It's less "generate a disposable game" and more "co-develop an engine."



Short version: HTML frameworks are great for disposable browser games. Argos is for an LLM-native, deterministic, native engine you extend over time.



\*\*"Ok but Godot has GodotIQ now, and Unreal has a Claude plugin — isn't that the same thing?"\*\* It's the opposite thing, and the distinction is the whole point. Those are AI \*assistants bolted onto a human-centric engine\*: the model reads and writes the engine's native files (\`.tscn\`/\`.gd\`, Blueprints, C#), a human reviews the output, the engine compiles (seconds to minutes), and if it crashes a human debugs it. The LLM is a smart coworker standing \*outside\* the engine, and however good its spatial or code intelligence gets, it can still emit something that's wrong, fragile, or non-deterministic — because it's generating open code.



Argos inverts the relationship: the engine's native interface \*is\* the LLM. The model is a conductor operating \*inside\* the build process, composing against a validated vocabulary the engine enforces — and invalid output can't ship by construction. It's rejected before it runs, not reviewed after. Valid output hot-reloads in \~0.5 seconds without stopping the sim. That's not something you retrofit onto Unity, Unreal, or Godot — it's engine-for-AI instead of AI-for-engine, a different design from the ground up.



\## Honest scope



Primitives are fantastic for fast, LLM-generated arcade games. For something deeper (a colony sim, a tactics game, a research tree), you'll need to add a few heavyweight system-primitives of your own first — but the architecture supports it, and crucially: if you build new systems as proper components whose state serializes (the same discipline that makes save/load work), you keep determinism and the multiplayer path intact. It's not an arcade-only dead end; it's a grounded base you extend.



\## This is for you if



You want to experiment with LLM-driven game development, you like the idea of an engine you and an AI grow together, and you're happy to fork and build. Take it in the arcade direction, or take it deep — both are legitimate.



Repo: [https://github.com/joel-gennari/argos](https://github.com/joel-gennari/argos)

Stack: C++20 · Lua 5.4 (sol2) · SDL3 · Dear ImGui · ENet · CMake/Ninja
